Yes, and we'd love it. Morphit publishes a stable public REST + SSE API (documented at `/v1/openapi.json` on any instance) covering the orderbook, profiles, feedback, and chat. Wallet developers can embed a Morphit orderbook screen directly in their wallet UI — the way Mycelium famously integrated LocalBitcoins back in the day — so users can browse and respond to peer-to-peer offers without leaving the wallet they already trust.

**What you can build with the API:**
- Filtered orderbook view scoped to whichever assets your wallet supports (BTC-only, XMR + BTC, multi-coin, etc.)
- Counterparty reputation lookup by account name — feedback count, average rating, account age
- Order detail pages with payment-method, amount, region, terms
- Encrypted chat threads routed through the user's existing Blurt posting key (you handle the UX; Morphit handles the cryptography)
- Federation-aware fetching — query any operator's instance, or your own; the orderbook is the same chain-backed data

**What we recommend:**
- Use Morphit's `@morphit/indexer-client` TypeScript workspace package if you're in a JS/TS stack — it's type-checked against the OpenAPI schema
- Cache responses with the published `ETag`/`Last-Modified` headers; the SSE stream tells you when state changes so you don't need to poll
- For maximum independence, point your wallet at a self-hosted Morphit instance or a community-run one; federation means the user gets the same orderbook either way
- The API is open and free; we ask only that you keep the Morphit orderbook attribution visible in the UI ('powered by Morphit P2P') so users know what they're looking at

If you'd like help, drop into our Matrix room (#agorise:matrix.org) or open an issue at git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit. The API is AGPL-3.0 like the rest of the project; integrators ship in their own license, and the network effect is mutual — every wallet that embeds Morphit's orderbook is an additional discovery path for new traders, and every new trader is a counterparty available to existing wallet users.

how_to_spread_morphit.q: How do I get people to use Morphit?
how_to_spread_morphit.a:
Word of mouth is the entire growth strategy. Morphit doesn't advertise, doesn't run promoted content, doesn't pay influencers — but every operator and supporter who brings a few people to the platform makes the orderbook materially more useful for everyone. Here are the channels that have worked, ordered roughly cheapest-effort-first:

**1. Online channels (free).**
- **Blog write-ups** on Blurt.blog (publish in the same ecosystem you're trading in — and earn Blurt for the post), Substack, Medium, Ghost, Mirror, or your own site. Deep-dive posts about Morphit, Blurt, and the broader cypherpunk fiat-to-crypto problem age well: linkable, citable, evergreen. Cross-post to Hacker News, Lobste.rs, the Monero subreddit, and any community where on-topic.
- **meetup.com groups** for crypto, Bitcoin, Monero, privacy, libertarian, freedom-tech, mesh-networks, and adjacent topics — many have monthly meetups where a 5-minute show-and-tell of the Morphit app is welcome
- **University clubs and billboards** — student cryptography clubs, libertarian student groups, computer science societies. Pin a printed QR-code-to-/install poster.
- **Existing privacy/security communities** like KYCnot.me, PrivacyGuides forums, Monero subreddit/Matrix, GrapheneOS discussions

**2. Physical channels (small printing cost).**
- **Flyers handed out at factory gates during quitting time** — many workers have unbanked or underbanked cash needs that crypto-no-KYC solves, and they're stationary in a line for 60 seconds where you can hand them something
- **Flyers on cars in parking lots, on doors, on community corkboards** in coffee shops, libraries, makerspaces, freedom-tech events. Keep the QR code big and the call-to-action one line ('Buy crypto, no ID' / 'Sell crypto for cash')
- **Stickers** on laptops at conferences, on lampposts in tech-heavy neighborhoods. Cheaper than flyers per impression

**3. Cross-promotion (free).**
- **Other crypto communities**: Ethereum, DeFi, Solana, XRP, Pirate Chain, Decred — each has its own user base, and Morphit trades all of them. A 'we trade your favorite coin too, peer-to-peer no KYC' angle lands well
- **Non-crypto communities** with overlap on values: libertarian groups, voluntaryist meetups, privacy advocates, sound-money / hard-money advocates, freedom-tech and mesh-network communities, agorist circles. Morphit is built specifically for the values these communities already hold

**4. Paid local promoters (operator-level, modest spend).**
- Pay a local crypto-curious 'geek marketer' a small base salary in pesos (or whatever your local currency is) plus performance commissions paid in Blurt. The peso salary keeps them committed; the Blurt commissions align them with the network's long-term growth and give them a free-speech-token stake. Commission events that work: new account signup (small bounty), first successful trade (larger bounty), demoing the app at a meetup (event-based bounty)
- This is exactly the kind of distributed grassroots marketing where Morphit's federation model shines — every operator can build their own local promoter network, independent of any central marketing budget

**5. What NOT to do.**
- Don't spam Telegram groups, Discord servers, or subreddits where you're not a regular. Crypto communities have strong spam-immunity reflexes and you'll burn the brand
- Don't pitch Morphit to people who already have a CEX account and are happy with it; pitch to the unbanked, the privacy-conscious, the people who've had CEX accounts frozen
- Don't promise things Morphit doesn't promise (no instant arbitration, no escrow, no guaranteed liquidity) — overselling drives churn

The federation model means every successful local promotion grows the network for everyone. A meetup attendee who joins through your operator instance is a counterparty available on every other operator's instance simultaneously. Local growth is worldwide growth.

totp_2fa_what_is_it.q: What is two-factor authentication and how do I enable it on Morphit?
totp_2fa_what_is_it.a: Two-factor authentication (2FA) means you need TWO pieces of evidence to unlock your Morphit keystore: your password (something you know) plus a rotating 6-digit code from a phone app (something you have). On Morphit, 2FA is completely optional — Morphit will NEVER require it, nag you to enroll, or warn you that your account is "insecure" without it. To enable it, go to Settings → Two-factor authentication, install one of our recommended open-source authenticator apps (Aegis, 2FAS, or Ente Auth), scan the QR code, and save the 10 backup codes somewhere safe. Honest about what it does: 2FA on Morphit blocks shoulder-surfing, borrowed-device replay, and casual local malware. It does NOT add cryptographic strength against an attacker who has both your encrypted keystore AND your password — the TOTP secret lives in the same encrypted blob as your keys. For that threat model, the path forward is FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys, which Morphit has exploratory support for.

totp_2fa_lost_authenticator.q: I lost my authenticator app — how do I get back in?
totp_2fa_lost_authenticator.a: When you enrolled in 2FA, Morphit showed you 10 backup codes and required you to acknowledge that you saved them somewhere safe (a password manager, printed and locked away, or written on paper). At the unlock screen, type one of those backup codes instead of a 6-digit authenticator code — the unlock field accepts both. Each backup code works exactly once; the keystore automatically marks it used and re-saves before letting you in. If you used all 10 backup codes and also lost your authenticator, your only path back is your 12-word seed phrase — Sign out, then on the welcome screen choose "I have a seed phrase," type the 12 words, and set a new password. Your keys are derived from the seed, so this recovers everything exactly. There is no Morphit admin who can reset your 2FA — Morphit doesn't hold your keys, so we genuinely cannot help if you lose all three: authenticator, backup codes, and seed.

totp_2fa_why_not_google_authenticator.q: Why doesn't Morphit recommend Google Authenticator?
totp_2fa_why_not_google_authenticator.a: Three reasons. First: closed source. We can't verify what it does with your secrets and you can't either. Second: cloud backup. Since 2023, Google Authenticator syncs your 2FA secrets to your Google account by default — opt-OUT, not opt-IN — and those secrets are not end-to-end encrypted to a password you control. That means anyone who compromises your Google account (phishing, SIM swap, Google losing a key, a subpoena) gets all your 2FA secrets at once. Third: the whole point of 2FA on a privacy-respecting marketplace is that the second factor stays separate from your main accounts. Recommending an authenticator that syncs to Google defeats the purpose for the exact user population (privacy-conscious Bitcoin and Monero traders) who chose Morphit specifically to avoid that pattern. Morphit recommends open-source apps where YOU control where the backup goes: Aegis (Android, encrypted local backups), 2FAS (iOS + Android, optional opt-in cloud backup), or Ente Auth (cross-platform, end-to-end encrypted sync). If you already have an authenticator you trust that isn't on our list — KeePassXC's TOTP, Bitwarden Authenticator, Yubico Authenticator, andOTP — that's fine. The recommendations are "what we suggest to a new user," not a denylist for anything else.

privacy_coins_onchain.q: How does Morphit keep my privacy-coin trades private?
privacy_coins_onchain.a:
Morphit trades several privacy coins — Monero (XMR), Zcash (ZEC), Pirate Chain (ARRR), Dash (DASH), and Decred (DCR) — and applies the same on-chain-footprint protections to all of them.

**Your actual settlement never touches Blurt.** When you trade a privacy coin, the coins move peer-to-peer between your wallet and your counterparty's, directly on that coin's own chain. That transfer is never broadcast to, recorded on, or visible from the blockchain Morphit coordinates on. Blurt only carries the public order (the advertisement) and the end-to-end-encrypted chat.

**What the order on Blurt reveals — and what we've stripped from it:**
• The order is an advertisement, so its side/asset/amount-range/payment-methods are necessarily public (that's how a buyer finds your sell). This is inherent to any public orderbook.
• But we removed everything that didn't need to be there: the order's permlink is now an opaque random token (`order-…`), not `sell-xmr-usd-…`, so the asset name no longer leaks into the on-chain permlink, order URLs, RSS feeds, or block explorers. The expiry timestamp is floored to the day, so it can't fingerprint the exact moment you posted. No IP, no timezone, no language, no browser fingerprint is ever attached — what you type into the "Post Now" form is all that goes on chain.

**Amount jitter on every coin.** When you share a receive amount in chat, Morphit adds a tiny random tail (down to the coin's smallest unit — piconero for XMR, satoshi-scale for the others) so the on-chain amount can't be matched to your posted order. On by default.

**ZEC, ARRR, DASH, and DCR are trade-only — their TxID never appears on Blurt at all.** You can't pay Morphit's listing fee with them, and the settlement is peer-to-peer, so there is no point at which any of those coins' transaction IDs are written to the public chain. For these four, the on-chain story is even cleaner than Monero's.

**Monero has exactly one optional cross-chain touch, with an opt-out.** XMR is one of three assets (with BLURT and BTC) you *may* use to pay the small listing fee; if you do, that fee payment's TxID is recorded in your order on Blurt (so any operator can verify the fee using a Monero tx_proof — no view key, see the Monero TxID FAQ). That is the only place an XMR TxID ever touches Blurt, and it's a ~$0.25 fee to a public address, never your trade. Want zero Monero-to-Blurt linkage? Pay the listing fee in BLURT — it's the default and half the price.

For the full per-coin guidance see /privacy/{asset} (e.g. /privacy/xmr, /privacy/zec), and the complete leak inventory lives in the project's metadata-leak catalog.

what_is_barter.a:
Barter lets you buy or sell goods and services — not cryptocurrency — and settle in crypto. A grandmother selling baskets, a neighbor who fixes bikes, someone trading a crate of oranges: they list what they're offering, price it in their local currency, and pick which crypto(s) they'll accept (say XMR, BTC, and DOGE). It's **one listing**, not one per coin.

**How it works:** describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms, set a local-currency value (a single price or a range), and tick the crypto(s) your town actually uses. Buyers browse the wares like any other listing and can only pay in a crypto you accept — if you don't list Decred, nobody can pay you in Decred. You and the buyer arrange the handoff in chat and settle in whichever accepted crypto they chose.

**No address on the listing:** the goods change hands off Morphit — in person or by post — so a barter listing has no crypto receive address, and Morphit never touches the goods or the payment. Common-sense safety applies: meet in a public place, share only what you need to, and treat a stranger like a stranger.

On Morphit, Barter is **trade-only** — you can't pay Morphit's listing fees with it (those stay Blurt/BTC/XMR). It's for trading wares, nothing else.

active_key.title: Active key
active_key.body: One of the three private keys your Morphit account has. The active key is for moving BLURT — paying listing fees, sending tips, transferring balances. Morphit asks for it (or rather, for the password that unlocks it on your device) only when you're about to spend. It never leaves your browser.

blockchain.title: Blockchain
blockchain.body: A blockchain is a shared record book that thousands of independent computers each keep a full copy of — instead of one company keeping it on a single server. Once something is written in, no single party can quietly erase or rewrite it, because every copy would have to agree to the change. Morphit settles on a blockchain (called Blurt) so your orders, ratings, and messages live somewhere no operator — and no government — can secretly alter or take down. That's what makes Morphit hard to censor or shut off: there's no central database for anyone to seize.

blurt.title: BLURT
blurt.body: BLURT is two things: a blockchain (where Morphit's order ops, fees, and chat ciphertext live), and the asset you pay listing fees with. The asset and the chain share the same name. There is no Morphit token — Morphit uses BLURT directly.

blurt_power.title: BLURT Power (BP)
blurt_power.body: BLURT that you have "powered up" — staked into your account so it can't be spent immediately and it earns you a passive income from staking your BLURT coins. BP gives you weight when voting on Blurt content (separate from Morphit) and is the basis for delegation. Morphit doesn't require any BP; it matters mainly if you syndicate trade announcements to the wider Blurt community.

broadcast.title: Broadcast
broadcast.body: To send a signed operation to the blockchain. Posting an order, cancelling an order, leaving feedback, sending an encrypted chat message — all of these are broadcasts. Once a broadcast lands in a block, it can't be undone (the operation is on-chain forever); only superseded by a later one.

counterparty.title: Counterparty
counterparty.body: The other person in a trade. If you posted a sell order and someone messages you to buy, that person is your counterparty. The word is neutral — it doesn't mean "opponent." Both sides of every Morphit trade have a counterparty: each is the other's.

custom_json.title: custom_json
custom_json.body: A type of operation on the blockchain that carries arbitrary structured data. Morphit's order ops, feedback ops, chat envelopes, and operator registrations are all custom_json operations — they ride on the chain's existing infrastructure rather than requiring a new chain. You don't need to interact with custom_json directly; Morphit builds them for you.

delegation.title: Delegation
delegation.body: Lending some of your BP to another account temporarily, without giving them control of your underlying BLURT. Morphit doesn't require delegation to use, but operators sometimes delegate to new accounts to give them initial weight. Delegations can be undone (with a cooldown period before the BP becomes liquid again).

federation.title: Federation
federation.body: Multiple independent Morphit instances that share the same orderbook and chat ecosystem because they all read from the same underlying blockchain. If one operator goes offline (or hostile), users move to another and find the same orders, the same trades, the same reputations. Federation is what makes Morphit uncensorable.

feedback.title: Feedback
feedback.body: A signed, on-chain rating you leave for a counterparty after a trade. Feedback is permanent — it can't be deleted, only responded to. Your reputation in Morphit is the sum of feedback others have left for you over time. Both sides of every completed trade are entitled to leave one piece of feedback.

fiat.title: Fiat
fiat.body: Government-issued currency: dollars, euros, yen, pesos, rubles. The opposite of crypto. On Morphit, fiat is what changes hands off-platform — you and your counterparty agree on a price in fiat (e.g. USD), settle the fiat side privately (cash, bank transfer, your choice), and Morphit handles only the crypto side.

indexer.title: Indexer
indexer.body: The component of a Morphit instance that watches the chain, decodes Morphit-relevant operations (orders, feedback, chat envelopes), and serves them to the web frontend in a usable shape. The chain is the source of truth; the indexer is just a fast cache. Run by the operator, not by you.

instance.title: Instance
instance.body: A single Morphit website, run by one operator — the site you're on right now is one instance. Because Morphit is federated, many independent instances all read the same blockchain and show the same orders, trades, and reputations. If one instance blocks you or goes offline, you can switch to any other instance and pick up exactly where you left off.

listing_fee.title: Listing fee
listing_fee.body: The small BLURT fee Morphit charges when you post a new order. The fee covers operator costs and disincentivizes spam orderbooks. The first order from a new account is free. Listing fees scale gently with how often you post. Cancelling an order does NOT refund the listing fee — it's the cost of the listing, not the trade.

network_fee.title: Network fee
network_fee.body: Two unrelated things share this name in casual speech: (1) Morphit's listing fee — the BLURT cost of posting an order; and (2) the Bitcoin or Monero on-chain fee that miners take when you settle the crypto side of a trade. Morphit only ever charges the first; the second is between you and the underlying network when you make the actual transfer.

operator.title: Operator
operator.body: The person or team running a particular Morphit instance — the website you're looking at right now is operated by someone. The operator runs the indexer and relay servers, sets policies for their instance (rate limits, fee tiers, kill-switch), and earns a share of the listing fees that flow through. If an operator goes hostile, you can switch to a different instance and find your same orders, same trades, same reputation.

password.title: Password
password.body: What unlocks your private keys on your device. Morphit never sees, sends, stores, or knows your password — it's used locally by your browser to decrypt the encrypted bundle of keys held in your browser's storage. If you forget your password, the keys are gone; that's why Morphit asks you to write down your seed phrase during onboarding.

permlink.title: Permlink
permlink.body: The unique short identifier of an order on the blockchain — something like `morphit-o-2k4f9`. Permlinks let you (and the chain, and other Morphit instances) refer to a specific order without ambiguity. The order's URL on any Morphit instance ends in its permlink, so order links are portable across instances.

posting_key.title: Posting key
posting_key.body: Another of your account's three private keys. The posting key is for signing content — chat messages, feedback, comments. It's lower-trust than the active key (it can't move BLURT) so a compromise is less catastrophic. Morphit uses it for chat-payload signing and feedback ops; you'll never need to handle it directly.

relay.title: Relay
relay.body: The component of a Morphit instance that handles things the indexer can't — chat envelope acceptance, fee verification, kill-switch enforcement, anti-spam policies. The relay is the moving-parts side of an instance (the indexer is read-only against the chain). Run by the operator, not by you.

release_op.title: Release op
release_op.body: An on-chain operation broadcast by the @morphit account that publishes the bundle hashes for a new Morphit release. Frontend pages use it to verify they're running unmodified code: each page hashes its own bundle and checks that the hash is signed off in a recent release_op. If the hashes don't match, the page warns you that the operator may be serving tampered code.

seed_phrase.title: Seed phrase
seed_phrase.body: Twelve English words that, taken together, are the master backup of your account. From the seed phrase your device can re-derive every key your account has. If your device dies and you lose your password, the seed phrase is what gets you back in. Write it down on paper. Don't take a screenshot. Don't email it to yourself. Don't store it in a password manager that lives on the same device.

sign.title: Sign
sign.body: To attach a cryptographic signature to a piece of data using one of your private keys, proving the data came from you and hasn't been altered. When Morphit asks you to "unlock to sign," it's about to ask the chain to accept an action on your behalf — posting an order, sending a message, paying a fee. The signing happens locally on your device; the private key never leaves.

glossary.heading: Glossary
glossary.intro: Plain-language explanations of the words Morphit uses. If a term in the UI is confusing, it should be defined here. If it isn't, please file an issue report.
glossary.footnote: These definitions are deliberately short. For longer or more technical answers, see the {faqOpen}FAQ{faqClose}.

home.hero_title: Anonymously trade cryptocurrencies, fiat, goods, services and more
home.hero_body: Morphit connects buyers and sellers directly. No KYC, non-custodial, no cookies, E2EE, no logging, no escrow, private by default, open source, fully-distributed

privacy.title: Privacy first
privacy.body: No KYC, email, phone/SMS, cookies, analytics or selfies. Pick a cool username, that's it, seriously.

true_p2p.title: True P2P
true_p2p.body: Assets move directly between Buyer and Seller only. No exchange wallet, escrow, arbitrators or middleman.

unstoppable.title: Unstoppable by design
unstoppable.body: Reachable on clearnet, Tor, Lokinet, I2P, Nostr and Federated instance runners. Block one and many others remain.

discoverability.title: Discoverability
discoverability.body: Federation uses an open public blockchain and RSS for orderbook distribution, trade finalization and user reputation.

encrypted_chat.title: Encrypted Chat
encrypted_chat.body: Buyer/Seller conversations are 100% private, E2EE and immutable for posterity in case you have a future dispute.

reputation.title: Reputation is everything
reputation.body: Use any number of different websites and your good reputation follows you. Your personal trades are always there.

trade_anything.title: Trade anything
trade_anything.body: 16+ cryptos plus direct goods, services and even barter. Cross-asset, cross-network, cross-medium.

instances.title: Known Morphit instances
instances.intro: Morphit is federated. Anyone can run an instance, and your indexer discovers other instances automatically by reading the chain. This list shows their current health from the most recent probe.
instances.bookmark_tip: 💡 Tip: bookmark a few of these instances — and their Tor, I2P, or Lokinet addresses — in your browser. The orderbook lives on the public blockchain, so if any one site is ever blocked or goes offline, you can reach the very same orders and trades through any other instance.
instances.add_yours_body: Run a Morphit instance? Just register on-chain — every other Morphit indexer will discover you automatically. The wizard (morphit-ops init) handles registration during first-time setup.

status_desc.good: Reachable, healthy, and synced within the lag threshold.
status_desc.quiet: Healthy, but no orderbook activity in the last 7 days.
status_desc.syncing: Reachable and healthy, but still catching up to the chain. Turns Good once synced.
status_desc.stale: Reachable, but its health check is degraded — a real problem on that instance.
status_desc.unreachable: Couldn't be reached over the network on the last check.
status_desc.mismatch: Reachable, but its operator account or treasury addresses don't match the canonical chain values.
status_desc.never: Queued — the probe hasn't checked this instance yet.

instances.empty_body: Your indexer is still catching up to chain head, or no operators have registered with an origin yet. Check back later.
instances.no_match_body: No instances currently have this status — try a different filter.

welcome_back.body: Unlock your encrypted keystore with the password you set up.
welcome_back.alternatives_body: No password reset — Morphit is non-custodial and nobody can recover it. But if you wrote down your 12-word seed phrase, you can still sign in with that.
welcome_back.yubikey_only_body: This keystore is locked to a YubiKey. Plug yours in and tap to unlock.
welcome_back.yubikey_browser_unsupported: YubiKey unlock requires Chrome, Edge, Brave, or another Chromium browser. You can also use your seed phrase to enter.

mailing_address_modal.intro: Share a physical address with your trade partner so they can ship goods or mail cash. Stays in this encrypted chat only.
mailing_address_modal.privacy_e2ee: This address is end-to-end encrypted in chat — only you and your trade partner can read it.
mailing_address_modal.privacy_irreversible: Sharing is irreversible: once sent, your partner has your address even if you clear the message later.
mailing_address_modal.privacy_pobox_tip: Consider using a P.O. box, mail-drop service, or virtual mailbox instead of your home address.
mailing_address_modal.privacy_clear_chat: After the trade completes, consider clearing this conversation history on both ends.
mailing_address_modal.country_help: Two-letter ISO country code (e.g. US, DE, JP).

my_orders.empty_body: When you're ready, posting an order takes about a minute.

cancel.confirm_body: This removes your order from the orderbook, so no one new can respond to it — and it can't be undone. Any chats you've already started stay open, and no one is charged. If you paid a listing fee, it isn't refunded.

no_account.title: Set up to see your orders
no_account.body: Your orders are stored on-chain under your Morphit identity. Create one to start trading, or unlock an existing identity to view your history.

locked.title: Unlock to view your orders
locked.body: Your order history stays behind your unlock, so a locked device never reveals your trades. Enter your password to view it.

fee_status_banner.heading: Fee status
fee_status_banner.body: Each order below shows its listing-fee status. An order appears in the public orderbook only once its fee is verified — a badge reading “not received”, “underpaid” or “not yet verified” is why an order may be missing there.

onboarding.title: Let's set up your keys
onboarding.intro: Your Morphit account is a pair of cryptographic keys. They are made right here on your device and never leave it. If you lose them, no one can recover them — not even us. That's the price of true privacy.

path_reputation.title: Build Reputation
path_reputation.body: One identity over time. Your successful trades earn a public track record that makes people trust you. Recommended for most users.

path_anonymous.title: Maximum Anonymity
path_anonymous.body: A fresh identity every trade. Nothing links your trades together. Best for Monero users who prioritize unlinkability — but you start from zero reputation every time.

onboarding.generating: Generating your keys securely on your device…
onboarding.generated_body: Before you do anything else, back them up. If you lose them, your account is gone forever. We warned you — this is the tradeoff for keys only you control.
onboarding.this_is_you: This is how you appear to others (unless you change it later)

backup.title: Back up your keys
backup.seed_hint: 12 words. In order. On paper. In KeePass(.info). Make a backup copy too. Store the 12 words somewhere SAFE. Do not photograph them. Do not email them to yourself.
backup.confirm_wrote_down: I wrote the seed down on paper
backup.confirm_understand: I'll keep these 12 words safe — I know they're the only way back into my account.
backup.password_hint: Choose a strong passphrase. This encrypts the backup file — not the keys on Morphit.
backup.continue: I've backed up my keys — continue
backup.blocked: Please confirm both boxes before continuing.
backup.password_too_short: Password must be at least 10 characters.
backup.keyfile_explain: Optionally download an encrypted backup of your keys. Same password as above. Store the file somewhere safe (USB drive, cloud you trust, another device) as an alternate path back into your account if the browser storage is wiped.
backup.password_strength_common: This password is among the most common — pick something unique to you.
backup.password_strength_trivial: Sequential or repeated patterns are easy to guess. Mix it up.
backup.persist_failed: Couldn't save your encrypted keystore to this device. Storage may be unavailable. Choose 'Seed every time' instead, or try again.
backup.password_strength_too_simple: Mix in numbers, symbols, or uppercase — or make it 12+ characters.

print_card.aria: Print a paper backup card with your 12 words
print_card.helper_hint: Opens your browser's print dialog. You can print to paper or save as PDF.
print_card.title: My Morphit backup card
print_card.subtitle: Keep this paper safe — it is the only way back into your account.
print_card.warning_body: Anyone who finds these 12 words can take everything in your Morphit account. Store this paper somewhere only you can reach — a safe, a locked drawer, or a secure deposit box. Don't photograph it. Don't email it. Don't store it in cloud notes.
print_card.instructions: If you ever lose access to your device, type these 12 words into Morphit's import flow on a new device to recover your account.

backup.keys_intro: These let you use this account in other Blurt apps. Your 12 words are still your main backup.

import.title: Import existing keys
import.body: Already have a Blurt account? Pick how you have your key stored. If you've never used Blurt before, [[go back]] and create a new account instead.
import.seed_hint: For users who set up Morphit (or another wallet that ships our seed format) before. If you don't have a 12-word seed, use one of the other tabs.
import.keyfile_hint: An encrypted .json file you exported from Morphit on another device, or a backup you saved.

posting_only.warning_body: If you don't have a 12-word seed or a Keyfile, just paste your Posting Key here instead. We'll encrypt it on this device for you. You'll be able to read, post, and trade with others, but NOT get discounted listing fees.
posting_only.wif_hint: Starts with a 5. Never shared with the operator — encrypted on this device only.
posting_only.new_password_hint: At least 8 characters. Used to unlock Morphit on this device. Not your Blurt password.

error.passwords_mismatch: Passwords don't match. Please retype both.
error.account_not_found: We detected your account (@{account}) but couldn't load it from Blurt just now. Check your connection and try again.

wif.too-short: That WIF is too short to be a valid Blurt key.
wif.too-long: That WIF is too long to be a valid Blurt key.
wif.bad-charset: WIF contains unexpected characters. WIFs use Base58 (no 0, O, I, or l).
wif.bad-version: That doesn't look like a Blurt private key.
wif.bad-checksum: WIF checksum failed — there's a typo somewhere. Re-copy and try again.
wif.bad-length: WIF is the wrong length to be a valid Blurt key.
wif.bad-scalar: Decoded successfully but the key is mathematically invalid. Re-copy and try again.

wrong_role.active: That's your Active key, which controls funds and account changes. For your safety, Morphit signs in with your Posting key only. Please paste your Posting key instead.
wrong_role.owner: That's your Owner key — the most powerful key on your account, and the one to guard most carefully. Morphit only ever signs you in with your Posting key. Please paste your Posting key instead.
wrong_role.memo: That's your Memo key — it's only used to encrypt and decrypt private messages and can't sign you in. Please paste your Posting key instead.

error.could_not_resolve: We couldn't detect your account from this key. Double-check that you copied your Posting Private Key correctly, or import with your 12-word seed or Keyfile instead.

posting_only.manual_account_hint: We couldn't detect your account from this key — it may be from before Blurt existed. Type your Blurt username so we can confirm the key belongs to it.
posting_only.manual_account_invalid: That username doesn't match this key. Check the spelling, or that you pasted the right Posting Private Key.

error.seed_word_count: A Blurt seed phrase is exactly 12 words — you've entered {count}. Make sure all 12 are present, each separated by a single space.
error.seed_invalid: That seed phrase isn't valid — one or more words aren't from the standard seed word list, or a word was mistyped. Check each word carefully and try again.
error.keyfile_password_wrong: That password doesn't match this keyfile. Passwords are case-sensitive, so check Caps Lock and any stray spaces, then try again.
error.keyfile_corrupt: This file isn't a valid Morphit keyfile, or it's been damaged. Upload the 'morphit-keyfile-….json' file you saved when you created your account — not a screenshot or a different file.
error.generic: Something unexpected went wrong while signing you in — it wasn't your key or password. Please wait a moment and try again.
error.network: We couldn't reach the Blurt network to verify your key. This is a connection problem on the network side, not a problem with your key. Check your internet and try again in a moment.

remember_me.body: Your keys are loaded for this browser session. By default, when you close this tab the keys disappear and you'll need your 12-word seed phrase again next time. If this is your own computer, you can choose to remember you on this device behind a password instead.

remember_me.password_hint: At least 8 characters. Used to unlock Morphit on this device.

plan.heading: What we're building
plan.subtitle: The plan is public. We ship in phases so every piece is done well.
plan.phase_1_body: The shell, the ten languages, the keygen flow, the searchable help — everything a first-time visitor needs, without any server-side account.
plan.phase_2_body: Connect to the chain. Ship the relay service that broadcasts user-signed operations. Release-discovery pointer lands on-chain.
plan.phase_3_body: Indexer goes live. Browse, filter, and post orders. 15-minute replace window. Sybil-resistant fee escalation. Self-trade detection.
plan.phase_4_body: End-to-end encrypted chat. Signed feedback with buyer/seller roles. Public reputation profiles.
plan.phase_5_body: Live BTC / XMR / BLURT payment flows. Tor, Lokinet, and I2P hidden services. IPFS release mirror. PWA + Federated instances onboarding.
plan.phase_6_body: Developers can embed a scoped orderbook screen into their UI. Users can search/browse/respond to offers without leaving the UI they trust.

asset_explainer.btc: Bitcoin (BTC) — the original cryptocurrency, used worldwide. Public ledger; transactions are visible. Network fees and confirmation time vary with network demand.
asset_explainer.xmr: Monero (XMR) — privacy-first cryptocurrency. Hides amounts, sender, and recipient by default. Ideal if privacy matters to you.
asset_explainer.blurt: BLURT — the social blockchain Morphit runs on. Fast (3-second blocks), zero-fee transfers, built-in rewards system. Perfect for reputation-building, trade posterity and connecting with like-minded people.
asset_explainer.usdt: Tether (USDT) — a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to USD. Centrally controlled — Tether Inc. can freeze any address.
asset_explainer.bch: Bitcoin Cash (BCH). Forked from Bitcoin in 2017 to favor bigger blocks and lower per-transaction fees over fee-market dynamics. Transparent ledger like BTC; no issuer can freeze addresses. Trade-only on Morphit — listing fees still paid in BLURT, BTC, or XMR.
asset_explainer.ltc: Litecoin (LTC). Forked from Bitcoin in 2011 with faster 2.5-minute blocks and Scrypt mining. Transparent like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses.
asset_explainer.dash: Dash (DASH). Forked from Litecoin in 2014 with masternode-coordinated services. Transparent at the base layer like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses. Optional PrivateSend mixing (a CoinJoin variant coordinated by masternodes) provides opt-in privacy.
asset_explainer.usdc: USD Coin (USDC) — a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to USD, issued by Circle. Centrally controlled — Circle can freeze any address.
asset_explainer.dai: DAI is a USD-pegged stablecoin by MakerDAO. More decentralized than USDT/USDC at the contract level (no admin freeze) but partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module.
asset_explainer.doge: Dogecoin (DOGE). Launched 2013 as a fair-launch fork of Lucky Coin (itself a Litecoin fork). Transparent at the base layer like Bitcoin — every transaction is publicly visible on the chain. No central issuer; nobody can freeze your addresses. Merge-mined with Litecoin since 2014 (auxiliary proof-of-work).
asset_explainer.zec: Zcash (ZEC). Launched 2016 as the first practical deployment of zero-knowledge proofs in a cryptocurrency. Transparent and shielded address types coexist on the same chain — t1/t3 addresses are publicly visible like Bitcoin's legacy addresses, while zs1 (Sapling) and u1 (Unified Address with Orchard receivers) use zk-SNARKs to hide sender, recipient, and amount. Choose the address type that matches your trade's privacy posture.
asset_explainer.arrr: Pirate Chain (ARRR) — chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool; every transfer is private by construction. Single address format (zs1 Sapling, bech32, 78 chars). Trade-only on Morphit; listing fees stay BLURT/BTC/XMR.
asset_explainer.dcr: Decred (DCR). A coin whose community votes on how the project is run. Its public ledger is visible like Bitcoin's, and its wallet has an optional privacy mode. No central issuer — nobody can freeze your coins.
asset_explainer.sol: Solana (SOL) — high-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency. Native SOL transfer (not wrapped SOL or SPL tokens). 32-44 character base58 addresses (same shape as USDT-Solana and USDC-Solana addresses; asset field disambiguates).
asset_explainer.eth: Ethereum (ETH) — Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency. Native ETH transfer (not wrapped ETH or ERC-20 tokens). 42-character 0x-prefixed hex addresses (same shape as USDT-ERC20, USDC-ERC20, DAI-ERC20, and every EVM token-account address; asset field + network field disambiguate).
asset_explainer.xrp: Ripple (XRP) — Federated Byzantine Agreement cryptocurrency on the XRP Ledger. 24-34 character base58 addresses starting with `r`. Destination tags (32-bit integers) are required when sending to exchange-hosted addresses — your peer-to-peer counterparty typically does not need one. XRPL accounts need ≥1 XRP base reserve to exist.
asset_explainer.barter: Barter (goods/services). Not a cryptocurrency — you offer wares or a service and get paid in the crypto(s) you choose to accept. Price it in your local currency; you and the buyer work out the details in chat and settle in one of your accepted cryptos. Describe exactly what you're offering in the Terms field.

form.waiver_fiat_hint: 💡 Most BLURT trades on Morphit happen with active Blurt social-network users, existing operators, or via barter. So, pick the fiat denomination that you use locally (USD, EUR, MXN, etc), and offer In-Person or Barter (goods/services) payment methods on Step 3 if you want to offer something else of value.

success.waiver_title: Your free first order is live!
success.waiver_body: It's already broadcast to the blockchain and visible in the orderbook to everyone — Morphit covered the listing fee for you. ❤️
success.waiver_step_1: Someone interested in trading BLURT for what you're offering will message you. You'll see a notification on the chat icon in the header — keep an eye out.
success.waiver_step_2: Chat to confirm terms (price, payment timing, location). When you're ready, share your BLURT receiving address (use the address-share button in the chat); they send you BLURT, you send them whatever you agreed to in return.
success.waiver_step_3: Once both sides confirm receipt, leave each other star-rating feedback. That feedback is permanent and what unlocks your 10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power welcome bonus from Morphit.
success.feature_upsell_heading: Want more eyes on this listing?
success.feature_upsell_body: Bid for a featured slot to put your order at the top of the orderbook for a few hours. The minimum bid is 6 hours; the rate is set per-instance. Most operators ship 50 BLURT/hour as the default.
success.edit_window_tooltip: Edits are only possible within 15 minutes of posting. After that, cancel and re-post.

broadcast_error.title: The order didn't go through
broadcast_error.body_generic: The chain didn't accept your broadcast. Nothing was paid. Try again or check your connection.
broadcast_error.body_insufficient_funds: Your account doesn't have enough BLURT to pay the listing fee.
broadcast_error.body_locked: The session is locked. Unlock your password to try again.
broadcast_error.body_bad_password: That password didn't unlock your keystore. Try again.
broadcast_error.body_posting_only: Paying the listing fee in BLURT needs your active key, and it isn't on this device — you're signed in with your posting key only. Sign in with your master password or full keyfile to pay in BLURT, or go back and pay in BTC/XMR (or use your free first listing).
broadcast_error.body_recipient_missing: The listing fee couldn't be sent — the treasury account it pays to (@morphit-fees) doesn't seem to exist on Blurt yet. Nothing was paid. If you run this instance, that account needs to be created; otherwise, please report this.
broadcast_error.body_insufficient_rc: Blurt takes a small network fee for this action from your liquid BLURT, and your account could not cover it. Top up a little liquid BLURT (incoming transfers are free) and try again. Nothing was paid.
broadcast_error.body_authority: Blurt rejected the signature on the fee payment — your account's Active key may not match what's on-chain. Nothing was paid. Try signing in again with your 12-word seed or Keyfile.

waiver.heading: Your first order is on us!
waiver.body: Welcome to Morphit! Your first order is a free BLURT buy. We cover the listing fee, and the BLURT you receive funds your future listings at the discounted BLURT rate, lets you vote on Blurt social content for curation rewards, and unlocks your 1 BP welcome stake.

fee_method.xmr_hint: Send the fee to our Monero address, then paste the transaction ID and proof below.

fee_method.tx_proof_placeholder: Paste the proof string from your wallet (starts with OutProofV1 or OutProofV2)

fee_method.tx_proof_malformed_length: Proof string is too short or too long. Generate a fresh one from your wallet.
fee_method.tx_proof_malformed_charset: Proof contains characters that don't belong. Copy it cleanly from your wallet's proof dialog.
fee_method.tx_proof_hint: Your wallet generates this for free. The proof reveals only this one payment — no other wallet activity.
fee_method.tx_proof_tooltip: A short string from your Monero wallet that proves you paid this specific transaction to our address — without revealing anything else about your wallet. Click for per-wallet instructions.
fee_method.tx_proof_privacy_note: Privacy: this proof reveals only this one payment to this address. It does NOT reveal your other transactions, your balance, your other addresses, or any wallet metadata.

fee_method.tx_proof_how_to_cli_body: Run: get_tx_proof <your-txid> <our-address>. The wallet prints a long string starting with OutProofV2 — copy that.

fee_method.tx_proof_how_to_cake_body: Settings → Privacy → Verify a transaction → Generate proof. Fill in the txid and our address; copy the proof.
fee_method.tx_proof_how_to_feather_body: Tools → Prove/check transaction → Generate. Fill in the txid and our address; copy the proof string.
fee_method.tx_proof_how_to_other_body: Most modern Monero wallets have a "Prove transaction" or "Generate proof" feature in their advanced or privacy settings. Look for it under Tools, Privacy, or Advanced. See the FAQ entry on payment proofs for the full explanation.

privacy.index_intro: Most assets traded on Morphit (BTC, BCH, LTC, DASH, DOGE, ZEC, ARRR, DCR, SOL, ETH, XRP, BLURT, USDT, USDC, DAI) live on transparent chains — any observer can read the chain history. There are concrete steps you can take to make YOUR trades much harder to link, profile, or surveil. This is registry-driven: the next asset Morphit adds will get a guide automatically.
privacy.section_fresh_addresses: Use a fresh address every trade
privacy.section_opt_in_tech_intro: Standards that wallets in this ecosystem may implement. Morphit does NOT recommend specific wallet software — even reputable wallets have been compromised. Search for a wallet that supports these standards and review its trust posture yourself.
privacy.no_wallet_recommendation: Morphit does NOT recommend specific wallet software. Even reputable wallets have been compromised or have had hidden flaws. The privacy techniques here are protocol standards, not endorsements — your wallet, your responsibility.

fresh_address_advice.subaddress: This chain supports stealth/subaddress technology natively. Your wallet derives a fresh receive address (subaddress) per trade from your view key. The recipient sees a unique address every time; chain observers cannot link multiple trades to the same wallet.
fresh_address_advice.hd-derived: This chain uses transparent addresses with no native stealth. The standard practice: use a Hierarchical Deterministic (BIP-32) wallet that derives a new receive address per request. Most modern wallets do this automatically. The cost of address reuse is severe — every trade you accept at the same address builds a public record of your activity.
fresh_address_advice.account-reuse: This chain is account-based — your account name is your address. Fresh-account-per-trade is not practical (each new account costs chain resources). Accept that this asset has the highest amount-correlation risk on Morphit. For high-value trades, consider using an alt-account dedicated to that trade.

mweb.name: MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks)
mweb.explain: A native Litecoin protocol-level privacy feature. MWEB hides transaction amounts and breaks the address-to-amount link for transfers that opt in. Per-transaction; not chain-wide. Look for wallets that surface "MWEB" or "Extension Blocks" as an option when sending.

cashfusion.name: CashFusion
cashfusion.explain: A Bitcoin Cash CoinJoin variant designed by the BCH community. Mixes inputs and outputs of varying amounts to defeat both common-input-ownership and amount-correlation heuristics. Run from a wallet that supports CashFusion before or after a trade to launder the on-chain history.

coinjoin.name: CoinJoin
coinjoin.explain: A family of protocols where multiple participants pool inputs and outputs into a single transaction, breaking the common-input-ownership heuristic that links coins to one owner. Multiple implementations exist with different trust models — choose carefully and read the implementation's threat model.

payjoin.name: PayJoin (BIP-78)
payjoin.explain: A two-party cooperative transaction protocol. Sender and receiver both contribute inputs, so chain observers cannot apply the standard "all inputs come from the same wallet" heuristic. Morphit's address-share modal includes an optional PayJoin endpoint field — if both wallets support BIP-78, the trade automatically uses PayJoin.

privatesend.name: PrivateSend
privatesend.explain: Dash's native CoinJoin variant. Uses denominated input/output amounts and masternode coordination to mix coins among multiple participants, breaking the link between sender and receiver on-chain. Run multiple mixing rounds (more rounds = larger anonymity set = higher fee). Pre-mix in your Dash wallet BEFORE sharing the address — by the time the funds reach Morphit they're already mixed.

shielded-pools.name: Shielded pools (Sapling + Orchard)
shielded-pools.explain: Zcash's protocol-level privacy. Shielded transactions (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address) use zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Sapling is the established shielded pool (since 2018); Orchard is the newer pool (Network Upgrade 5, 2022) accessed through Unified Addresses. Per-address — recipients pick z/u-addr for shielded transactions or t-addr for transparent. Both transparent and shielded are first-class on the protocol. Wallets that fully support shielded sends: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk Wallet (mobile, Sapling). Older wallets may only support transparent (t-addr) sends, so confirm your counterparty's wallet supports the address type you intend to use.

csppmix.name: CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing
csppmix.explain: A wallet-side mixing protocol that bundles your transaction inputs with other participants in a single multi-party round.  After mixing, your outputs are no longer linkable to your original inputs on chain.  Integrated into dcrwallet for Decred — enable the "Mix Account" option.  Opt-in (you choose when to mix); off-protocol (mixing rounds aren't enforced by consensus).

common_practices.fresh_per_trade: **Use a fresh receive address for every trade.** Your wallet should support this; if it doesn't, look for one that does. Address reuse is the single biggest leak.
common_practices.coin_control: **Practice coin control when spending.** When sending coins later, avoid combining the trade output with coins from another source — that combines their address histories permanently.
common_practices.network_layer: **Broadcast through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode.** Your home IP address sees the transaction first; nodes near your IP can correlate it to you. A Tor-aware wallet broadcasts through Tor by default.
common_practices.kyc_touchpoints: **Avoid sending trade coins to or from KYC exchanges.** Once trade coins touch a KYC exchange, the trade becomes legally identifiable by combining exchange records with chain data. If you need to bridge to fiat, route through a self-custodied intermediate step.

what_not_to_do.reuse_address: Do not paste your same receive address into multiple trades.
what_not_to_do.exact_amount: Do not send the exact amount listed on the order — Morphit's amount-randomizer toggle (the "🔐 Randomize amount" checkbox in the address-share modal) breaks this; leave it ON.
what_not_to_do.combine_utxos: Do not combine the trade output with coins from a different source when you later spend it.
what_not_to_do.clearnet_broadcast: Do not broadcast from your home IP via a non-private wallet — use Tor.

btc.one_line: Transparent chain, fully decentralized — opt-in mixing protocols available.
btc.intro: Bitcoin is the most-analyzed chain in the world. Every transaction is public; every address can be tracked over time. The privacy practices below dramatically reduce how easily a third party can profile your trades — without requiring you to leave BTC.
btc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, PayJoin, CoinJoin, and what to avoid.

xmr.one_line: Privacy by default — stealth addresses, hidden amounts, ring signatures.
xmr.intro: Monero's chain-level privacy hides sender, recipient, and amount by default. By default, your address, amount, and counterparty are hidden from third parties. The practices below are minor tightenings; the chain itself does the heavy lifting.
xmr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Monero trades on Morphit: subaddresses and amount handling.

blurt.one_line: Coordination chain — transparent and account-based. Lowest privacy on Morphit.
blurt.intro: BLURT is Morphit's coordination chain — orders, chat ciphertexts, fees, and reputation all live here. The chain is fully public and account-based, meaning every BLURT transfer involving your account is permanently visible to anyone. There is no opt-in privacy technology for BLURT.
blurt.caveats: BLURT is structurally the least private asset on Morphit. Your account name is your address; you cannot rotate it. For trades where on-chain privacy matters more than speed and cost, prefer XMR, BTC (with PayJoin), BCH (with CashFusion), LTC (with MWEB), or DASH (with PrivateSend).
blurt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for BLURT trades on Morphit: account-based chain, transparent by design.

usdt.one_line: Centralized — Tether can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdt.intro: USDT's privacy issue is structurally different from the other transparent assets: it's centralized. Tether Inc. can freeze any USDT address on any host chain, and they have used this ability in the past. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Tether's freeze capability.
usdt.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDT remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDT host chains (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BSC) is the same as on any transparent EVM/UTXO/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem (Tornado Cash on ETH, etc.), which we do not endorse or describe further here.
usdt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDT trades on Morphit: centralization risk and host-chain transparency.

bch.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — CashFusion provides opt-in mixing.
bch.intro: Bitcoin Cash shares Bitcoin's transparency model: every transaction visible on chain, every address linkable. CashFusion (a BCH-community CoinJoin variant with amount-randomization) is the main opt-in privacy technology and is well-integrated into several BCH wallets.
bch.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin Cash trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, CashFusion, and what to avoid.

ltc.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — MWEB provides opt-in chain-level privacy.
ltc.intro: Litecoin shares Bitcoin's transparency at the base layer, but adds MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks) — a chain-level opt-in privacy feature that hides amounts and breaks address linkability for transfers that opt in. This is the closest a Bitcoin-family chain comes to native privacy.
ltc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Litecoin trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, MWEB, and what to avoid.

dash.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized — PrivateSend provides masternode-coordinated opt-in mixing.
dash.intro: Dash forked from Litecoin in 2014 and shares the same transparent base layer — every address balance and transaction is publicly visible. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer can freeze addresses. Dash adds PrivateSend, a CoinJoin variant coordinated by the masternode network, providing opt-in mixing at the wallet level. Pre-mixing several rounds before sharing your receiving address is the strongest privacy practice on Dash.
dash.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dash trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, PrivateSend pre-mixing, and what to avoid.
dash.caveats: PrivateSend's anonymity set depends on simultaneous mixing participants. Off-peak hours = smaller set = weaker unlinkability. Masternode coordination is a trust trade-off: the protocol is non-custodial (masternodes never hold your coins) but the coordinator sees the mixing pattern.

usdc.one_line: Centralized — Circle can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdc.intro: USDC's privacy posture mirrors USDT's: it's centralized. Circle (USDC's issuer) can freeze any USDC address on any host chain, and has done so on regulatory request. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Circle's freeze capability. The amount-correlation defense (jitter) IS active for USDC trades — see /{lang}/faq#monero_amount_jitter — but jitter addresses a different threat than centralization.
usdc.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDC remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDC host chains (Ethereum, Solana, Base, Polygon) is the same as on any transparent EVM/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem, which we do not endorse or describe further here. BEP-20 USDC on BNB Chain is intentionally NOT supported: that variant is Binance-Peg (Binance-custodied wrapper of Circle-issued USDC), adding a second custodian to the existing one.
usdc.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDC trades on Morphit: centralization risk, host-chain transparency, and the amount-jitter defense.

dai.one_line: DAI — USD-pegged stablecoin governed by MakerDAO. No admin freeze on the token, but partly backed by USDC.
dai.meta_description: Honest privacy notes for trading DAI on Morphit: more decentralized than USDT/USDC at the contract level, partly backed by USDC via the Peg Stability Module.
dai.intro: DAI is MakerDAO's USD-pegged stablecoin, deployed on Ethereum and several other EVM chains. It's the most-decentralized US-dollar-pegged asset Morphit supports — but "decentralized" doesn't mean "freeze-immune" or "fully crypto-backed" anymore. This page is the honest picture so you can choose with eyes open.

doge.one_line: Transparent base layer, decentralized via PoW, no native privacy upgrade.
doge.intro: Dogecoin launched in 2013 as a fair-launched fork of an earlier Litecoin variant. Like Bitcoin, every address balance and transaction is publicly visible on the chain. The chain is fully decentralized; no issuer or foundation can freeze addresses. Since 2014 it has been merge-mined with Litecoin (auxiliary proof-of-work), inheriting Litecoin's hashrate security without competing for it.
doge.meta_description: Privacy practices for Dogecoin trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, avoiding chain heuristics, and what tradeoffs to expect.
doge.caveats: Dogecoin has no native privacy upgrade — no PrivateSend equivalent, no confidential transactions, no segwit-enabled mixing. Every receive address you publish on Morphit can be linked to its on-chain history forever. Use a fresh HD-derived address for every trade (your wallet usually does this automatically).

zec.one_line: Transparent and shielded address types coexist; recipients pick per address.
zec.intro: Zcash launched in 2016 as the first deployment of zk-SNARK-based shielded transactions in a cryptocurrency. The chain supports two address families: transparent (t1/t3) which behave like Bitcoin's legacy addresses with publicly visible amounts, and shielded (zs1 Sapling, u1 Unified Address bundling Orchard receivers) which use zero-knowledge proofs to hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Per-trade, the recipient picks the address type that matches their preferred posture. Both are first-class on the protocol.
zec.meta_description: Privacy practices for Zcash trades on Morphit: choosing between transparent and shielded addresses (t-addr, z-addr, u-addr), wallet recommendations, and what each privacy pool does.
zec.caveats: Shielded-to-shielded transactions hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain. Mixed transactions (shielded-to-transparent or transparent-to-shielded) reveal one side. Transparent-to-transparent reveals both. If your goal is to minimize linkability, use a shielded address (zs1 or u1) and ask the counterparty to send from a shielded address. Wallet support varies: Zashi (mobile, official from Electric Coin Co, Sapling + Orchard), Zecwallet (desktop, Sapling), Nighthawk (mobile, Sapling) — not every wallet supports every address type, so verify your counterparty's wallet handles the address type you publish before sharing it.

arrr.one_line: Chain-level shielded transactions via the Sapling zk-SNARK pool; every transfer hides sender, recipient, and amount by construction.
arrr.intro:
Pirate Chain (ARRR) launched in 2018 as a fork of the Zcash codebase, configured so that the Sapling shielded pool is the only available transaction type.  Every transfer goes through zero-knowledge proofs (zk-SNARKs) that hide sender, recipient, and amount on chain.  Pirate Chain sunsetted the transparent pool early in the chain's life and forcibly migrated all transparent balances to shielded — there is no transparent address option.  Addresses use the `zs1` Sapling format (bech32, 78 chars total), visually identical to Zcash Sapling addresses.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene that survives even chain-level shielding — the on-chain payload is private, but what you share off-chain (which addresses you publish, which counterparties you transact with) is what links your Morphit trades together over time.
arrr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Pirate Chain trades on Morphit: chain-level shielded transactions, fresh-address hygiene, and wallet compatibility.
arrr.caveats:
Pirate Chain's chain-level shielding hides sender, recipient, and amount on chain — but it does not erase off-chain linkability.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `zs1` address across multiple Morphit listings lets observers correlate your orders even though the chain itself reveals nothing.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Pirate Chain wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Wallet compatibility.**  Not every wallet supports Pirate Chain (the major options are Treasure Chest, Pirate.Black, and Verus-integrated Pirate).  Confirm your counterparty has a compatible wallet before agreeing to a price.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Visual collision with Zcash Sapling addresses.**  Pirate Chain `zs1` addresses look exactly like Zcash `zs1` addresses.  Morphit's per-asset tab and placeholder disambiguate, but if you copy an address from a different context, confirm it belongs to the chain you intend to send on.

dcr.one_line: Hybrid PoW/PoS cryptocurrency with on-chain governance (Politeia) and opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) wallet-side mixing.
dcr.intro:
Decred (DCR) launched in 2016 as a hybrid Proof-of-Work + Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with on-chain governance.  Every block is mined by PoW miners AND voted on by 5 PoS ticket-holders chosen pseudo-randomly from the staking pool — neither group can change the protocol rules unilaterally.  On-chain governance via Politeia lets stakeholders propose, debate, and ratify protocol changes; treasury funds (10% of block reward) flow through community vote.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Decred ships an opt-in CoinShuffle++ (CSPP) mixing protocol integrated into dcrwallet: users can enable mixing in their wallet to break the on-chain transaction graph between deposit and withdrawal, similar in posture to Bitcoin coinjoin or Dash PrivateSend.

The practices below cover wallet-side hygiene to make the most of Decred's privacy features.
dcr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Decred trades on Morphit: hybrid PoW/PoS chain, on-chain governance, opt-in CoinShuffle++ wallet mixing, and fresh-address hygiene.
dcr.caveats:
Decred is transparent at the base layer; mixing is opt-in and wallet-side.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same `Ds` or `Dc` address across multiple Morphit listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade (Decred wallets derive these from your HD seed).
- **Use CSPP mixing if you want transaction-level privacy.**  In dcrwallet enable the "Mix Account" option; deposits flow through CoinShuffle++ rounds with other participants before becoming spendable from your mixed account.  Mixing rounds happen approximately every 20 minutes on mainnet.
- **Wallet compatibility.**  The official wallets are dcrwallet (CLI/headless), Decrediton (GUI), and Cake Wallet (mobile, DCR mode).  Some other wallets support DCR send/receive but not CSPP mixing.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Politeia treasury proposals are public.**  Decred's on-chain governance system shows every proposal, vote, and discussion publicly.  This isn't a Morphit-trading concern, but worth knowing if you participate in DCR governance.

sol.one_line: High-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency with Proof-of-History sequencing.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
sol.intro:
Solana (SOL) launched in 2020 as a high-throughput Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency.  Validators stake SOL and process blocks in rotation under delegated PoS consensus, with Proof-of-History providing a verifiable sequencing oracle that lets validators reach consensus on transaction ordering without coordination overhead.  The combination achieves transaction throughput several orders of magnitude higher than traditional UTXO chains while remaining decentralized — no central freeze authority controls the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Solana has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
sol.meta_description: Privacy practices for Solana trades on Morphit: high-throughput PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped SOL, and RPC provider considerations.
sol.caveats:
Solana is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Solana address across multiple Morphit listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Solana wallets (Phantom, Solflare) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native SOL, not wrapped SOL.**  Wrapped SOL (wSOL) uses the SPL-token form for DEX interoperability; the mint address `So11111111111111111111111111111111111111112` is the famous wSOL identifier.  Morphit trades use NATIVE SOL transfers — sending wSOL to a SOL receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for Program-Derived Addresses (PDAs).**  PDAs are off-curve addresses controlled by on-chain programs, not by private keys.  If you send SOL to a PDA, the recipient can't move funds out unless the owning program has a withdraw instruction.  Most wallets show a warning before sending to a PDA; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as USDT-Solana and USDC-Solana.**  A Solana base58 address could be a native SOL account, a USDT-Solana token account, or a USDC-Solana token account — the format is identical.  Morphit's order asset field tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Solana RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Helius, QuickNode, Triton, public mainnet-beta) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a Solana RPC node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.

eth.one_line: Proof-of-Stake cryptocurrency on the Ethereum mainnet.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
eth.intro:
Ethereum (ETH) launched in 2015 as a smart-contract platform.  In September 2022 the chain transitioned from Proof-of-Work to Proof-of-Stake consensus ("The Merge") — validators stake ETH and process blocks in rotation, with no central freeze authority controlling the chain.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, and amount are visible on chain like Bitcoin.  Ethereum has no native protocol-level mixing protocol.  Tornado Cash was a notable smart-contract mixer but has been sanctioned in many jurisdictions; Morphit does not recommend or rely on it.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
eth.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ethereum trades on Morphit: PoS chain, transparent base layer, fresh-address hygiene, native vs wrapped ETH, contract-destination warnings, ENS limitations, and RPC provider considerations.
eth.caveats:
Ethereum is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same Ethereum address across multiple Morphit listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern Ethereum wallets (MetaMask, Rabby, Rainbow) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Send native ETH, not wrapped ETH.**  Wrapped ETH (WETH) is an ERC-20 token used for DEX interoperability.  Morphit trades use NATIVE ETH transfers — sending WETH to an ETH receive address requires the recipient to unwrap, which may not happen.
- **Watch for contract destinations.**  Ethereum addresses can be externally-owned accounts (EOAs, controlled by a private key) OR smart contracts.  Sending ETH to a contract without a `payable receive()` or `fallback()` function reverts; the funds aren't lost but the transaction fails and you pay gas.  Most wallets warn before sending to contracts; pay attention.
- **Same address shape as every EVM token-account.**  An Ethereum 0x-address could be a native ETH EOA, a USDT-ERC20 token-account, a USDC-Base token-account, a DAI-Polygon token-account, or any EVM contract.  The format is identical.  Morphit's order asset field (plus the network field for multi-network assets) tells you which one to send; double-check before signing the transaction in your wallet.
- **ENS names are not resolved.**  Pasting `alice.eth` will fail Morphit's address validator — paste the raw 0x address.  Resolving ENS would require a centralized RPC dependency that violates Morphit's distributed-no-SPOF design.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **Ethereum RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an RPC endpoint (Infura, Alchemy, QuickNode, public mainnet) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting an Ethereum node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Gas fees can leak timing.**  Ethereum gas prices vary by congestion.  Submitting a transaction during a high-gas window with a higher tip can correlate the tx to a specific time window.  Standard wallet defaults (medium priority) blend with the broader mempool.

xrp.one_line: Federated Byzantine Agreement cryptocurrency on the XRP Ledger.  Transparent base layer; wallet-side address rotation is the primary privacy lever.
xrp.intro:
Ripple (XRP) launched in 2012 as a payment-focused cryptocurrency.  XRPL uses Federated Byzantine Agreement (FBA) consensus — validators on a Unique Node List (UNL) reach agreement on transaction ordering.  The default UNL is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation (non-profit) with the for-profit Ripple Labs Inc. historically influencing validator selection.  Native XRP cannot be frozen by any central authority — the freeze flag on XRPL applies only to issued tokens (IOUs), not to native XRP.

The chain is transparent at the base layer — sender, recipient, amount, and destination tag (if present) are all visible on chain like Bitcoin.  XRPL has no native protocol-level mixing.  Users wanting transaction-level privacy rely on wallet-side address rotation (deriving a fresh address per trade from their HD seed) and off-chain coordination — the practices below cover what you can control.
xrp.meta_description: Privacy practices for Ripple (XRP) trades on Morphit: XRPL FBA consensus, transparent base layer, destination tag UX, reserve requirement, and RPC provider considerations.
xrp.caveats:
XRPL is transparent at the base layer with no native mixing protocol.

- **Share fresh addresses per trade.**  Using the same XRPL address across multiple Morphit listings lets observers correlate your orders on a fully transparent chain.  Generate a fresh receive address per trade — modern XRPL wallets (Xaman, Crossmark, Bifrost) derive these from your HD seed and let you create new accounts in seconds.
- **Destination tags are not a privacy feature — they're an identifier.**  If your counterparty asks for a destination tag and you supply one, that tag is visible on chain and can be used to correlate transactions.  For peer-to-peer trades the destination tag is typically not needed at all.  Only include a destination tag when the receiving address is an exchange-hosted omnibus wallet that requires one for routing.
- **Reserve requirement creates account-creation visibility.**  Your first incoming XRP must be ≥1 XRP (the base reserve).  The on-chain `Payment` transaction that funds a new account is publicly visible as account activation, which is a stronger correlation signal than a regular payment to an already-existing account.  If reducing this signal matters, fund the receive address yourself first (from an account that's already mixed/separated) and only then share it.
- **Network-layer privacy still matters.**  Broadcasting through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode keeps your home IP off the chain's view of you.
- **XRPL RPC providers can correlate.**  Your wallet talks to an XRPL RPC endpoint (xrplcluster.com, Ripple's, or a self-hosted rippled node) — that provider sees every transaction you sign.  Self-hosting a rippled node, or rotating between providers, reduces the surface area.
- **Consensus-set concentration is a known property.**  The default UNL (Unique Node List) is published by the XRP Ledger Foundation; running your own validator with a custom UNL is supported but uncommon.  For Morphit's purposes this affects censorship-resistance considerations (a coordinated UNL could refuse to include transactions) more than transaction privacy.  Document and decide based on your threat model.
- **X-addresses are not currently supported as a receive format.**  XRPL has a newer "X-address" format (XLS-5d) that bundles the destination tag into the address itself — Xaman/Xumm, Crossmark, Bifrost, and GemWallet all parse them.  Morphit currently accepts only classic `r`-prefixed addresses; if your counterparty asks for an X-address, share your classic address and the destination tag separately instead.  Adding X-address support is on the post-launch enhancements list.

privacy_terms.heading: Privacy & Terms
privacy_terms.privacy_body_1: Morphit runs in your browser. Your keys are generated on your device and never leave it. Morphit does not collect tracking cookies, analytics, or your IP address for any purpose beyond what's technically required to serve the page.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_2: Every offer you post — along with the feedback and reviews you leave and receive — is public on the blockchain, for reputation-building, posterity, and your own research on other traders.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_protected: By contrast, your private conversations stay private. Direct messages between traders are end-to-end encrypted — they live on the blockchain only as ciphertext that you and your trade partner can read, never the operator, the indexers, or anyone else watching the chain. Morphit also collects no name, email, phone, or ID, and the payment details you exchange (such as a receiving address) move through that encrypted channel instead of the public orderbook.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_3: We encourage you to use a VPN, Tor, Lokinet, or I2P when accessing Morphit — anything that hides your IP from the server you're talking to is a good idea. We don't fingerprint your browser, we don't profile you, and we explicitly design our defenses against abuse so they don't punish privacy-conscious users. Our rate limits are crude (a handful of signups per IP per day) and easily defeated by VPN rotation — that's a conscious tradeoff. We'd rather accept more abuse than make privacy-respecting users feel unwelcome. If a defense would require tracking you to work, we don't ship it.
privacy_terms.terms_body: Please abide by the Non-Aggression Principle (NAP). Cursing is acceptable, but just keep in mind that there are all ages that use Morphit. Elderly, teens and everyone in between. All OPINIONS are welcome here, but directed insults are not. Your Buy/Sell orders, the Feedback section and Chats are immutable, so wording is everything. State your opinion, then stop. Don't start fights. Do not post illegal or obviously objectionable stuff. Remember your manners, be nice. 💚💙

privkey_warn.explain: If you send this anyway, Morphit will automatically truncate the key so only the first 6 and last 4 characters go out. The full secret will not leave your device. But please — just remove it before sending.
